svg.aria-label: Diagram: Network Load Balancers in Google Cloud, passthrough and proxy compared; both operate at Layer 4 but they are opposite machines, the passthrough variety being explicitly not a proxy, delivering packets with source and destination addresses, protocol and ports unchanged, terminating connections at the backends and returning replies straight to the client as direct server return, while the proxy variety is a Layer 4 reverse proxy that terminates traffic at the load balancing layer and opens a fresh TCP connection to the closest available backend; the consequences diverge across every axis, with passthrough preserving the client address and carrying TCP, UDP, ESP, GRE, ICMP and ICMPv6 plus SCTP and AH internally, allowing up to five ports or a range or all ports per forwarding rule, and being unable to offload SSL at all so backends decrypt at their own CPU cost and Google-managed certificates are unavailable, whereas proxy carries TCP only, permits exactly one port per forwarding rule, can remap that port so a rule on 80 reaches a backend on 8080, offers TLS offload on the global external and classic modes, and relays the lost client address only if you enable the PROXY protocol; the global external passthrough balancer is built on Maglev, sends traffic to the region closest to where it entered Google's network, spills over to the next closest region when one is at capacity and fails over when one is down, and hands you two external addresses on deliberately disjoint availability groups AG0 and AG1; the internal passthrough balancer runs on Andromeda, is always regional, cannot balance internet traffic unless fronted by an external balancer, and does not handle IPv6 packets with fragmented headers; and target pools are the legacy backend, limited to TCP or UDP and external IPv4 only
svg.title: Network Load Balancers: two Layer 4 products that are opposite machines
svg.text: Same layer, same family name, opposite machines. One refuses to touch the packet;
the other replaces the connection entirely.
PASSTHROUGH — “as the name suggests … not proxies”
Packets arrive with “source and destination IP addresses, protocol, and … the source and
destination ports UNCHANGED”. “Load-balanced connections are terminated AT THE BACKENDS.”
Replies go “DIRECTLY to the clients, not back through the load balancer” — DIRECT SERVER RETURN.
So the load balancer sees the request and never the response. Half the conversation, by design.
Built on MAGLEV (external) and ANDROMEDA (internal) — not on GFEs, not on Envoy.
PROXY — a Layer 4 REVERSE PROXY, which is the opposite thing
“Traffic is TERMINATED at the load balancing layer and then forwarded to the closest available
backend by using TCP.” Two connections, as in #104. Replies return through the balancer.
“Intended for TCP traffic ONLY, with or without SSL.” No UDP, no ICMP, no ESP, no GRE.
For HTTP(S) Google recommends an Application Load Balancer instead — so this is for TCP that
is not HTTP: databases, brokers, custom protocols.
Where the two diverge, and it is every axis that matters
CLIENT ADDRESS — passthrough preserves it. Proxy loses it, and relays it back only if you
enable the PROXY PROTOCOL. That is a backend change, not a load balancer setting.
PORTS — passthrough: “up to five ports, a range of ports, or ALL ports” per rule.
Proxy: “EXACTLY ONE port from 1-65535” per rule — but it can REMAP it.
“The forwarding rule could use TCP port 80, while the connection to the backends … 8080.”
SSL — “The passthrough Network Load Balancer CANNOT perform this task.” Backends decrypt, at
“a greater CPU burden on the VMs”, and “Google-managed SSL certificates are ONLY available
for proxy load balancers”. Certificate management moves to you, permanently.
PROTOCOLS — passthrough carries 6 externally, 8 internally. Proxy carries 1.
What “global” means for a passthrough balancer
It “directs traffic to the backend region CLOSEST TO THE POINT WHERE USER TRAFFIC ENTERS”
Google’s network — the entry point, not the client’s location.
AT CAPACITY → “spills over SOME of the new user connections … to the next closest region(s)”,
“while KEEPING EXISTING CONNECTIONS in the current region”. DOWN → fails over outright.
“Each load balancer provides you with TWO EXTERNAL IP ADDRESSES, served by DISJOINT AND
ISOLATED … infrastructure (also known as availability groups, AG0 and AG1).”
Two addresses is not redundancy you add. It is redundancy you are handed, and must publish.
Internal passthrough: regional, and firmly so
Built on Andromeda. Premium Tier only. Widest protocol list in Google Cloud: TCP, UDP, ICMP,
ICMPv6, SCTP, ESP, AH and GRE. Global access controls CLIENT reach, never backend reach.
Does NOT support: “Backend VMs in multiple regions”; internet-origin traffic “unless you’re
using it with an external load balancer”; and “IPv6 packets with FRAGMENTED HEADERS”.
That last one is the kind of limit you only meet in production, on one path, intermittently.
Several forwarding rules may share one common IP address.
Choosing between them is not a feature comparison. Ask what must survive the hop: the CLIENT’S
ADDRESS, or anything other than TCP → passthrough. TLS OFFLOAD, PORT REMAPPING, or backends
outside Google Cloud → proxy. Both at once is not available, in either direction.
